subject: Performance SLO benchmark methodology & next steps

Subject: Performance SLO benchmark methodology & next steps

Hi Samir / Iris —

Thanks again for a productive call earlier today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can align the benchmark and SLO qualification:

Summary of EdgeFin targets (as discussed)
- Latency: p95 end-to-end response <= 300ms for small responses (<=128 tokens); streaming per-token latency target <= 150ms between token flushes for interactive flows.
- Throughput: sustain 200 QPS during peak windows; 60s sustained windows for measurement.
- Concurrency: support 40 concurrent open sessions with KV/cache reuse for prompt prefixes.
- Availability: tolerate graceful degradation to a smaller model variant with failover policy.

What we shared: attached is our benchmark methodology (Redwood_Benchmark_Methodology_v1.pdf) and a suggested prompt set (edgefin_prompt_set_v1.json) to mirror your user journeys.

Open questions / asks for your team:
1) Please confirm the workload shape in the attached edgefin_expected_workload.csv (esp. ratio of short vs. long responses).
2) Are there any streaming semantics (realtime flush frequency or chunk size) we should preserve exactly?
3) Can you provide a staging API key or short-lived access for our benchmark runners, or would you prefer we run from your environment?

Next steps proposed
- Ethan to validate measurement definitions and confirm harness details (ETA 1 business day).
- Redwood team to run an initial benchmark on a dedicated pool against the provided prompt set once workload file + access are confirmed.
- Follow-up sync to review results and any tuning (can be 30m).

Attachments: Redwood_Benchmark_Methodology_v1.pdf (PDF, 24KB); edgefin_prompt_set_v1.json (JSON, 18KB)

Thanks — looking forward to confirming the inputs and getting a run scheduled.

Best,
Marissa

Marissa —

Thanks for the detailed recap and the attachments. A few clarifications from our end before we hand over staging keys: 

1) Workload: attached is our expected_workload export (edgefin_expected_workload.csv). The primary peak is short interactive queries (60% < 64 tokens) with occasional long responses for batch summarization (~10%).
2) Streaming: our client expects token-by-token flushes roughly every 120-180ms; if your streaming harness emits tokens faster, that's fine — we care more about P99 token inter-arrival during interactive flows.
3) Measurement definitions: Can you confirm how you define p95 latency for streaming flows? Is that time-to-first-byte, time-to-last-byte, or inter-token percentiles?

We are happy to provide a staging API key scoped to the benchmark runner and can add Redwood IPs to a temporary allowlist. Samir will coordinate with our infra team once we agree on measurement definitions.

From: Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Performance SLO benchmark methodology & next steps

Hi Samir —

Thanks for the workload file and the streaming clarification. Quick technical definitions so we're all aligned; I'll also drop the benchmark harness links below.

Measurement definitions (Redwood benchmarking team):
- End-to-end response latency (p95 / p99): measured from when our ingress timestamp registers request receipt to when the client receives the final byte of the response (time-to-last-byte). For short, non-streaming flows we report time-to-first-byte and time-to-last-byte.
- Streaming token latency: we measure inter-token intervals for the streaming session. Per-token p95 is the 95th percentile of the observed intervals between consecutive token flushes across all sessions in the run. We will also report time-to-first-byte for the initial token separately.
- Throughput: sustained requests per second measured over sliding 60s windows; reported as median and 95th percentile of windowed QPS.
- Concurrency: concurrent open sessions measured as the instantaneous number of active sessions when issuing the request; we will sweep concurrency levels (10, 20, 40, 60) to show scaling characteristics.
- Reproducibility: each configuration will be run 3 times; we report mean and standard deviation. All raw traces (timestamps, token events) will be shared.

Benchmark harness / artifacts:
- Public harness repo (read-only for your team): https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmark-harness
- Shared drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3cRedwoodBenchmark (includes runner configs, Docker images, and run scripts)
- Expected measurement outputs: run_summary.csv, token_traces.parquet, latency_histograms.json (we will share these after each run)

Test environment we propose:
- Use Redwood Dedicated instance (Redwood-managed dedicated pool) to avoid noisy neighbors for initial runs; we can also run a follow-up in your staging VPC if you prefer. Model: redwood-llama-70b-q4 (quantized) to match inference cost/latency targets.

Next steps from Redwood engineering:
1) Once you confirm you can provide a staging API key (or prefer Redwood-managed dedicated), we'll schedule the first run.
2) We'll seed the harness with edgefin_prompt_set_v1.json and your workload CSV and run the 10/20/40 concurrency sweep.
3) Share raw outputs and a 30m review call to interpret results and discuss tuning (batching, cache policy, quantization profile).

If agreeable, please send the staging key (scoped / short-lived) or tell us to proceed on Redwood Dedicated. Happy to meet with your infra team to coordinate allowlist IPs.

Cheers,
Ethan Park
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
ethan.park@redwood.ai
